newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Young Singaporean seeks credible opposition voice.
newsitem.headline: Young Singaporean seeks credible opposition voice.

text.p: Many young, well-educated Singaporeans, brought up in comfort and detached from past struggles, say they want a credible opposition to check the long-ruling People's Action Party (PAP).
A lot of them will be voting for the first time in general elections on Thursday, which the PAP has already won because the opposition is standing in only 36 of parliament's 83 seats.
Young Singaporeans interviewed by Reuters said they were content with that situation, but would vote for the opposition if a "good candidate" were standing.

"We are not like our parents, saying yes to everything," said one taxi driver preparing to vote for the first time. He would not vote for the PAP, which has won every election since Singapore became self-governing in 1959.
Born after Singapoore's independence in 1965, these young folk are often criticised by their elders as a self-centred generation that does not fully appreciate the country's early hardships.
But that is why, analysts say, these voters, about a quarter of the 800,000 electorate in contested seats, may be more inclined to experiment with their votes, much to the concern of the PAP.
These voters in Singapore -- where voting is compulsory for everyone over 21 -- would be crucial in determining the extent of the opposition voice, the analysts said.
In the old 81-seat parliament, the opposition held just four seats. They hope to double that number on Thursday. The PAP is determined they will not.
"I would vote for the opposition just to get some sparks and action in parliament, some kind of an alternative voice," said student Simon Lok. "Parliamentary proceedings have been too smooth."
"I am all for the opposition to keep the ruling party in check, so they cannot get away with everything," said a 27-year-old journalist.
"For me, I still believe in the PAP. There is more stability and there is already a sense of trust," said Wixy Song, a 23-year-old student.
But she added: "I still think the opposition is necessary, for only if there is competition would there be improvement."
These young Singaporeans are less restrained in voicing their views that their elders, but most declined to be named.

"For Macpherson (one of the contested constituencies), it is quite straight-forward, the integrity of Chee is in ruins. How can one trust such a person?" asked a 29-year-old part-time student referring to Chee Soon Juan.
The government calls Chee, head of the Singapore Democratic Party (SDP), "a cheat and a liar".
Chee was one of four SDP leaders fined for contempt of parliament after mis-stating how much government spent on health care. Chee put the error down to a typing mistake.
"Don't fix something that is not spoilt," Dick Su, a 23-year-old actor, said in support of PAP's continued reign in power since 1959.
"The PAP has better leaders, smarter people, who would not trip on their own feet," Su said referring to Chee Soon Juan.
